@graph.headline: When to Quit a Strategy: How to Tell a Broken System From a Normal Drawdown

acceptedAnswer.text: Your strategy is no longer working when it breaks its own historical bounds: a drawdown deeper than its max historical depth, an underwater period longer than its longest, or a losing streak beyond its worst — combined with deteriorating rolling expectancy (last 30–50 trades vs full history, net of costs). No single number proves it; the combination of broken bounds plus a two-window expectancy decline is the practical verdict. Losing streaks alone are not evidence — they're usually normal variance.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my trading strategy is no longer working?

acceptedAnswer.text: You need enough trades for the statistics to mean something: at minimum 30–50 recent trades for a rolling expectancy read, and 100+ trades for a strong verdict (a 50%→30% win-rate collapse over 100 trades has roughly a 0.003% chance of being noise). One bad 30-trade window is almost always variance; two non-overlapping 30-trade windows both deteriorating is about a 1-in-400 event and worth acting on. There is no magic number — there are confidence levels, and they grow with sample size.

mainEntity.name: How many trades does it take to know if a strategy is dead?

acceptedAnswer.text: A drawdown is a loss within the system's historical bounds — deep, painful, but precedented. A broken strategy is one whose behavior has left its historical bounds: deeper drawdowns, longer underwater stretches, or structurally changed R-multiples than its own record shows. The practical difference: a drawdown in a live system is the price of admission you pay to collect the edge; a broken system has no edge left to collect. Your pre-written quit contract (the three numbers) is what tells them apart, because it was written when you could think clearly.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a drawdown and a broken strategy?

acceptedAnswer.text: More than you'd think. Exact math (dynamic programming, cross-checked by Monte Carlo): a 40% win-rate system has a median longest losing streak of 9 over 200 trades, and a 6-loss streak is 87% likely over 100 trades. Even at 50% win rate, the median is 7 over 200 trades. So no streak length by itself means the setup stopped working — streaks are terrible alarms. Use them as a prompt to check your three numbers and rolling expectancy, never as the verdict.

mainEntity.name: How many losing trades in a row means a setup has stopped working?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — strategy decay is real, and it's one of the best-documented phenomena in finance. In the published version of Hou, Xue & Zhang's "Replicating Anomalies" (Review of Financial Studies, 2020), 65% of 452 tested anomaly variables failed to clear the single-test significance hurdle (t = 1.96), and 82% failed the stricter multiple-testing hurdle (t = 2.78) — many edges that "worked" in-sample don't survive out-of-sample. (The replication debate has legitimate arguments on both sides, but the decay direction is well established.) Edges decay because markets adapt, crowds pile in, regimes change, and costs rise. The question was never whether setups stop working — it's whether yours has, which is what the protocol answers.

mainEntity.name: Do trading setups really stop working?

acceptedAnswer.text: Adjust only when you can name the specific structural change that justifies it — a regime shift, a rule change, a market-structure event. If you're hunting for a parameter that would have dodged the recent drawdown, you're fitting to noise: retire the system. And never adjust parameters mid-drawdown — do the work in calm, on fresh data, and reintroduce the system through forward testing. If you can't name a structural reason, retirement is the honest answer.

mainEntity.name: Should you retire a setup or adjust it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — dead regimes return. A trend system shelved in a sideways market can work again when trends return; a volatility setup starved in quiet ranges can feast when volume comes back. But "again" has to be earned, not assumed: write the post-mortem, set a re-examination date 6–12 months out, and demand fresh forward-test evidence (paper trading first) before re-sizing. A retired system never comes back at full size on nostalgia. And if the early "working" period was really luck on a flat-expectancy system, the right move is burial, not resurrection.

mainEntity.name: Can a retired trading setup start working again?

acceptedAnswer.text: Strategy decay is the gradual erosion of a trading edge over time: the same rules produce less expectancy per trade, smaller winners, or more frequent losses than their history. It happens because markets adapt (crowding arbitrages away the mispricing), regimes shift (the conditions the edge exploited disappear), or costs rise relative to the edge (fee drag eats a thinning margin). Decay is different from a drawdown (temporary, within bounds) and different from overfitting (the edge was never real). You detect it the same way you detect anything in the quit protocol: broken historical bounds plus deteriorating rolling expectancy with clean execution.
